item.title: 3D Audio - Introduction
item.description: 3D Sound 4.0. INTRODUCTION Imagine closing your eyes while standing on a busy street corner. In that instant, you can easily perceive cars passing from left to right, footsteps approaching behind you, someone speaking to your right, and an airplane passing overhead. Human hearing naturally localizes sounds in full three-dimensional space. The goal of 3D spatial audio technology is to recreate this rich acoustic sensation artificially over headphones or loudspeakers, making listeners perceive sound sources as originating from specific three-dimensional coordinates in space.

item.title: Computer Simulation & Implementation
item.description: 4.6. Implementation: Room Acoustic Simulation To create a realistic 3D acoustic simulation in software, we must synthesize not only the direct sound and HRTF cues, but also the reflective acoustic characteristics of an enclosed room. The Image Source Method A standard method for simulating room acoustics is Allen & Berkley’s Image Source Model. Each boundary wall acts as an acoustic mirror. For each physical reflection, a “virtual mirror source” is placed behind the reflecting wall at an equal distance.

item.title: Coordinate Systems
item.description: 4.2. COORDINATE SYSTEMS FOR SPATIAL AUDIO To precisely specify the position of a virtual sound source relative to the listener, spatial audio systems use spherical coordinate systems centered at the midpoint between the listener’s ears: The Three Spatial Dimensions: Azimuth ($\theta$): The angle in the horizontal plane, measured from the frontal line of sight ($0^\circ$). $0^\circ$: Directly in front $+90^\circ$: Directly to the right $180^\circ$: Directly behind $-90^\circ$ (or $270^\circ$): Directly to the left Elevation ($\phi$): The vertical angle relative to the horizontal plane.

item.title: Echoes & Reverberation
item.description: 3. ECHOES AND REVERBERATION In everyday listening, we are rarely aware of how much acoustic energy reaching our ears consists of reflections rather than direct sound. In enclosed spaces, the direct sound from a source is immediately followed by a dense series of reflections off walls, ceilings, floors, and furniture. Direct Sound and The Precedence Effect (Haas Effect) The direct sound travels in a straight line from source to listener and arrives first.

item.title: Head-Related Transfer Functions
item.description: 4.4. Head-Related Transfer Functions To determine the acoustic pressure that an arbitrary sound signal $x(t)$ produces at the eardrum, we require the acoustic impulse response $h(t)$ between the source position and the eardrum. This impulse response is known as the Head-Related Impulse Response (HRIR), and its Fourier transform is the Head-Related Transfer Function (HRTF). The HRTF encapsulates all physical cues used by the human auditory system to localize sound in three dimensions.

item.title: Introduction to Csound
item.description: 1. Introduction CSOUND is a computer software system designed to synthesize digital audio signals and facilitate computer music composition. Csound achieves precise, sample-accurate control over sound generation at every instant through two complementary files: Orchestra instruments: Programmatic routines that define the digital signal processing algorithms capable of generating and manipulating sound. Score events: A structured data file specifying when and how instruments are invoked, containing pitch, duration, amplitude, and spatial coordinates encoded in a standard numerical score format.

item.title: Spatial Audio Mechanisms
item.description: 4.1. Mechanisms of Spatial Hearing The human brain relies on several complementary physical and psychoacoustic cues to localize sound sources in three dimensions: 1. Interaural Time Difference (ITD) Because our ears are separated by approximately 17 to 20 cm of skull, sound originating off the median plane arrives at the closer ear slightly earlier than at the contralateral ear. The maximum ITD for a source directly to one side (azimuth 90°) is approximately 0.

item.title: Spatial Audio Systems
item.description: 4.3. SIMPLE SPATIAL AUDIO SYSTEMS Spatial audio reproduction systems are generally categorized by transducer configuration and delivery technique: 1. Two-Channel Stereo (Loudspeakers) Standard stereophonic setups use two loudspeakers positioned symmetrically in front of the listener (typically at $\pm 30^\circ$). By varying the relative gain between channels (panning / interchannel level differences), a “phantom center” or virtual source can be positioned between the speakers. Limitation: Virtual sources cannot be positioned behind, above, or around the listener without specialized acoustic crosstalk cancellation or multichannel surround arrays.
